topics.title: React Fiber Architecture & Reconciliation Engine
topics.summary: Deep dive into Fiber node structures, double-buffering, interruptible render phase, and heuristic O(n) diffing.
topics.content:
## React Fiber & Reconciliation Deep Dive

### The Stack Reconciler Bottleneck (React 15)
In React 15, reconciliation was synchronous and recursive. Once a tree update started, it could not be paused. If diffing a large tree took 40ms, the main thread froze, dropping frames below the 60fps budget (16.6ms/frame).

### The Fiber Solution: Cooperative Multitasking
Fiber re-implemented reconciliation as a **singly-linked list data structure** representing a unit of work. Work can now be:
1. **Paused** and resumed later
2. **Prioritized** (user input > background data fetch)
3. **Aborted** if superseded by higher priority updates

```
Fiber Node Structure:
├── type & tag: Function/Class component, HostComponent (div, span)
├── key: String identifier for list diffing
├── stateNode: Reference to actual DOM node or class instance
├── child: Pointer to first child Fiber
├── sibling: Pointer to next sibling Fiber
├── return: Pointer to parent Fiber
├── memoizedState: Linked list of hooks
└── alternate: Pointer to counterpart in double-buffering
```

### Double-Buffering Mechanism
React maintains two Fiber trees in memory simultaneously:
1. **`current` tree**: Represents the exact state currently rendered on screen.
2. **`workInProgress` (WIP) tree**: Built and modified during the Render phase.

```
Screen (User View)
       ▲
       │ (Atomic pointer swap in Commit Phase)
┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
│ current tree │ ◄──────► │ workInProgress tree  │
└──────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘
```

### Two-Phase Execution Pipeline

| Phase | Synchronous? | Interruptible? | Responsibility |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Render Phase** | No (Concurrent) | **Yes** | Traverses tree, runs component functions, builds WIP tree, computes flags (`Placement`, `Update`, `Deletion`). Discardable if higher-priority update occurs. |
| **Commit Phase** | **Yes** (Atomic) | No | Takes completed WIP tree, rapidly applies batch DOM mutations, executes `useLayoutEffect`, and swaps `current = workInProgress`. |

### Heuristic O(n) Diffing Rules
1. **Different Element Types**: Replacing `<div>` with `<span>` immediately destroys the entire old subtree.
2. **Keyed Lists**: Keys must be **stable, unique, and predictable**. Never use array index when items can be inserted, deleted, or reordered.

topics.title: State Management Architecture: Context vs Zustand vs Redux vs TanStack Query
topics.summary: Evaluate Client State vs Server State: Context API re-render traps, Redux Toolkit, Zustand atomic selectors, and TanStack Query caching.
topics.content:
## Modern Frontend State Management Architecture

### Client State vs Server State
The biggest mistake in modern frontend is treating Server Cache as Client State:
- **Server State**: Asynchronous, shared, remotely owned, requires caching, deduplication, background refetching (Use **TanStack Query / SWR**).
- **Client State**: Synchronous, local to client, ephemeral UI state (modals, active tabs, theme).

```
State Classification:
├── Server State (Async) ────► TanStack Query / RTK Query
└── Client State (Sync)
    ├── Local UI State ──────► useState / useReducer
    ├── Shared Subtree ──────► Context API
    └── Global Complex ──────► Zustand / Redux Toolkit
```

### Context API Re-render Trap
When a Context value changes, **every single consumer component re-renders**, even if it only reads an untouched property of the context object!

```jsx
// ❌ Re-render Trap: Header re-renders when cart changes!
const AppContext = createContext();

// ✅ Solution A: Split contexts by update frequency
const AuthContext = createContext(); // Changes rarely
const CartContext = createContext(); // Changes frequently

// ✅ Solution B: Atomic Selectors with Zustand
import { create } from 'zustand';

const useCartStore = create((set) => ({
  items: [],
  addItem: (item) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, item] })),
}));

// Only re-renders when items.length changes, not on unrelated updates:
const itemCount = useCartStore((state) => state.items.length);
```

### Comparison Matrix

| Library | Paradigm | Bundle Size | Boilerplate | Selective Re-rendering |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Context API** | Built-in React | 0 KB | Low | Poor (requires splitting) |
| **Zustand** | Store + Atomic Selectors | ~1.2 KB | Very Low | Excellent (selector subscriptions) |
| **Redux Toolkit** | Unidirectional Flux | ~11 KB | Medium | Excellent (`useSelector`) |
| **TanStack Query** | Server State & Cache | ~12 KB | Low | Automatic caching & invalidation |
topics.interviewTip: State management questions are a trap if you jump to Redux immediately. First separate Server Cache (TanStack Query) from Client UI State (Zustand).

topics.title: RxJS Operators Deep Dive: switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap
topics.summary: Master RxJS higher-order mapping operators for real-time autocomplete search, file uploads, queues, and button spam prevention.
topics.content:
## RxJS Higher-Order Mapping Operators

When an Observable emits items that trigger another inner Observable (e.g. user keystroke triggering an HTTP request), higher-order mapping operators determine concurrency behavior.

```
Comparison Summary:
├── switchMap  ──► Cancels previous in-flight inner observable (Search/Autocomplete)
├── concatMap  ──► Queues sequentially in order (Sequential DB writes)
├── mergeMap   ──► Runs all concurrently in parallel (Bulk uploads)
└── exhaustMap ──► Ignores new emissions while inner is active (Login/Submit button)
```

### 1. `switchMap` (Search & Autocomplete)
Cancels any previous HTTP request if a new value arrives before the previous request completed:
```typescript
searchControl.valueChanges.pipe(
  debounceTime(300),
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(query => this.http.get(`/api/search?q=${query}`))
).subscribe(results => this.results = results);
```

### 2. `exhaustMap` (Submit & Login Buttons)
Ignores clicks until the active HTTP request finishes. Eliminates double-submission bugs:
```typescript
loginButtonClicks.pipe(
  exhaustMap(() => this.authService.login(credentials))
).subscribe();
```

### 3. `concatMap` (Strict FIFO Queuing)
Waits for inner observable to complete before starting next:
```typescript
orderIds.pipe(
  concatMap(id => this.orderService.processOrder(id))
).subscribe();
```

### 4. `mergeMap` (Uncontrolled Concurrency)
Runs all inner observables in parallel. Can overload backend if concurrency is unrestricted:
```typescript
fileUploads.pipe(
  mergeMap(file => this.upload(file), 3) // Optional concurrency limit = 3
).subscribe();
```
topics.interviewTip: Remember this mental model: switchMap cancels, concatMap queues, mergeMap parallels, exhaustMap blocks.

topics.title: Core Web Vitals & Frontend Performance Optimization
topics.summary: Optimize LCP (<2.5s), INP (<200ms), and CLS (<0.1) across the Critical Rendering Path with code splitting and modern bundling.
topics.content:
## Core Web Vitals & Web Performance

### The Three Core Metrics

| Metric | Definition | Target | Common Culprits & Mitigations |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) | Render time of largest above-the-fold image/text block. | **< 2.5s** | Slow TTFB, render-blocking scripts, large hero images. Fix with preloading and `fetchpriority="high"`. |
| **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) | Page responsiveness to clicks, taps, keypresses (replaced FID). | **< 200ms** | Long JavaScript tasks blocking main thread. Fix with `scheduler.yield()`, web workers, and code splitting. |
| **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Unexpected visual layout shifts during session. | **< 0.1** | Images/ads lacking explicit aspect ratio, dynamic banner insertions. Fix with CSS `aspect-ratio`. |

### Critical Rendering Path (CRP) Optimization
```
1. HTML ──► DOM
                ├──► Render Tree ──► Layout (Reflow) ──► Paint ──► Composite
2. CSS  ──► CSSOM ──┘
```

- **`defer` vs `async`**:
  - `defer`: Downloads in background, executes in document order **after** DOM parsing is complete.
  - `async`: Downloads in background, interrupts parser and executes immediately upon download.
topics.interviewTip: Emphasize that INP evaluates the longest interaction throughout the entire session lifecycle, not just initial load.

topics.title: Frontend Security: XSS, CSRF & Token Storage Debate
topics.summary: Protect client-side applications against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), CSRF attacks, and implement secure JWT storage.
topics.content:
## Frontend Security Architecture ### 1. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Attacker injects malicious JavaScript executed in the user's browser session: - **Stored XSS**: Payload saved in database (e.g. comment field). - **Reflected XSS**: Payload embedded in URL search query. - **DOM-based XSS**: Insecure client script manipulation (`element.innerHTML = userInput`). ```javascript // ✅ Safe: React automatically escapes strings inside JSX
{userComment}
// ✅ Sanitization if rich HTML is mandatory import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
``` ### 2. JWT Storage Debate: LocalStorage vs HttpOnly Cookie | Storage | XSS Vulnerability | CSRF Vulnerability | Production Recommendation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **LocalStorage** | ❌ Vulnerable (Any JS snippet reads `localStorage.getItem`) | ✅ Immune (Cannot be sent automatically by browser) | Avoid for high-value session tokens | | **HttpOnly Cookie** | ✅ Immune to JavaScript theft | ⚠️ Vulnerable if SameSite not set | **Recommended**: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` | ### 3. Content Security Policy (CSP) HTTP response header restricting allowed script/media origin domains: ```http Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com; object-src 'none'; ```
topics.interviewTip: Explain why storing access tokens in memory (React state) + refresh tokens in HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookies is the gold standard for SPAs.
